newsitem.title: UK: Kvaerner to act on costs as profits slump 55 pct.
newsitem.headline: Kvaerner to act on costs as profits slump 55 pct.

text.p: Norwegian shipbuilding and engineering group Kvaerner ASA on Monday announced a 55 percent slump in pre-tax profits in the first nine months and said it was taking steps to cut costs by 1.1 billion crowns ($174 million) per year.

Kvaerner posted profits before tax of 851 million crowns compared with 1.9 million crowns in the corresponding 1995 period. Operating profits tumbled 45 percent to 912 million crowns against 1.66 billion crowns.
The results included five months operations from British conglomerate Trafalgar House, which Kvaerner acquired in April, and a gain of 258 million crowns from the sale of ships.
Kvaerner shares closed in Oslo two crowns up at 255 crowns.
Kvaerner said the aggregate result was unsatisfactory and it was taking action to improve under-performing businesses.

"The (pre-tax) figure is clearly a figure we are disappointed with and long term we must see completely different figures," Erik Toenseth, president and chief executive officer, told a news conference.
"There are some things we're happy with when it comes to individual results...but for the group we're unhappy..." he said.
Toenseth said the merger with Trafalgar House was progressing smoothly and Kvaerner continued to get closer to its objective of disposing of 10 billion crowns of non-core assets.
"We have identified a lot of synergies, some partly related to costs, but more important synergies in the fact that the businesses can support each other.
"That is coming through quickly, not without problems, but they (synergies) are starting to come through."

Toenseth said the company was implementing measures which would lead to cost savings of 1.1 billion crowns annually, including 200 million crowns per year from the reorganisation of the group's headquarters in London and Oslo, 200 million crowns from rationalisation of the merged company's international structure, 350 million crowns per year in the pulp and paper division and 350 million per year from increasing competitiveness in the energy division.
Shipbuilding remained Kvaerner's main profit contributor with a pre-tax result of 750 million crowns, down from 991 million crowns a year ago.

"We continue to see good results in shipbuilding. They are not as good as last year, but still very good, in an environment where our competitors are either going broke or being rescued again by their national government," the Kvaerner chief said.
He said yards at Govan in Britain and Kleven in Norway continued to struggle, while Warnow in Germany had improved productivity. Finland's Masa-Yards and Norway's Floroe remained the top performers.

Toenseth said a solution had been found for French subsidiary, Sofresid, which should return to profit next year. Generally market conditions for the John Brown business were strong globally, with the possible exception of Europe, he said.
Construction incurred a loss of 24 million crowns in the five-month period since the Trafalgar acquisition due to weak results in the British market.
Meanwhile pre-tax profits in the oil and gas business plunged to 24 million crowns against 163 million a year ago.
Kvaerner said the drop was caused by losses on contracts in Norwegian fabrication units and continued overcapacity.

Pulp and paper, another former core Kvaerner business, booked a loss of 199 million crowns against a loss of 70 million crowns. The losses were despite a 167 million crowns gain from the sale of Finnish Tampella Corp in the second quarter.
"Pulp and paper has been a big headache for us," Toenseth said. "We are doing something substantial to change the way we work by reducing costs and increasing efficiency..."
Kvaerner's figures fell mainly in line with expectations, but analysts said the management needed to show firm results.

"I see potential in the long term but the management needs to prove itself now. The share price should be cheaper because the fourth and first quarters (1997) are not going to be good," said an Oslo-based analyst. ($1=6.328 Norwegian Crown)
